title: Stereo pose diagnostics
lede: Two cameras, one 5-DOF pose. Each case shows the stereo pair the estimator saw, the back-projection geometry that produced the answer, and that answer against ground truth.

measurements:
Which part of the robot spoils the outline

The robot is not a flat ring — a rod sticks out one side of it and the body the other. Here the same poses are re-rendered with those parts deleted from the 3-D model, one at a time. Numbers are how far the outline bulges past a perfect ellipse, in pixels, on each of the two sides. If deleting a part makes the bulge vanish, that part caused it.

mesh25°40°55°65°70°
full mesh+1.4 / +0.2+2.1 / +0.4+2.8 / +0.5+3.3 / +7.0+4.5 / +10.6
mast removed+1.4 / +0.2+2.1 / +0.4+2.8 / +0.5+3.3 / +0.9+4.5 / +1.3
body removed+1.4 / +0.2+2.1 / +0.4+2.8 / +0.5+3.3 / +7.0+4.2 / +10.6
rim ring only+1.4 / +0.2+2.1 / +0.4+2.8 / +0.5+3.3 / +0.9+4.2 / +1.3

Removing the rod makes the second column collapse past 55°. Removing the body changes nothing at any tilt. The ring on its own reproduces the first column exactly. So below about 55° the error is not the rod or the magnet at all — it is that the ring itself has thickness, and a thick ring seen at an angle is wider than the flat circle the maths assumes.

The wall model

If the extra width really is the ring’s own thickness, then it should grow in a specific way as the robot tilts — in proportion to sin(tilt) — and dividing one by the other should give a flat line at the ring’s half-thickness. Measured on the ring alone: 0.408 mm.

Flat means the explanation is right. It also means the correction can be worked out from the shape of the robot rather than fitted to data — one number, the ring’s thickness, instead of a curve with arbitrary coefficients. The point below 20° drops off because the effect there is smaller than one pixel at this resolution.

The outline's centre is displaced too

the parts that stick out grow the outline on one side, so its centre moves — and sideways position is read straight off that centre. Displacement is split along the outline's own long and short axes.

tiltalong long axisalong short axisas distancewith one-sided re-weighting
10°-0.62 px+0.89 px0.346 mm0.346 mm
25°-0.56 px+0.94 px0.350 mm0.350 mm
40°-0.60 px+1.10 px0.399 mm0.400 mm
55°-0.61 px+1.13 px0.410 mm0.410 mm
65°-0.42 px-0.44 px0.195 mm0.208 mm
70°-0.35 px-2.38 px0.769 mm0.584 mm

Almost all of it is along the short axis — the direction things stick out in — while the long axis stays flat. The sign flips near 57°: below that the rim’s own thickness pushes the centre one way, above it the rod pulls it the other, so no single tilt-based correction can undo both. At 70° this displacement alone is 0.87 mm, past the 0.5 mm target. Re-weighting the outline only partly helps, and not at all below 55°, because the weights are judged against an ellipse that has already absorbed the shift. This is not yet corrected anywhere in the shipped estimator.

Which channels survive

How wrong each of the ellipse’s measurements is, compared with what geometry says it should be, grouped by how side-on that camera’s view of the robot is. This is the table everything else follows from.

how side-onsampleslong axis, lengthlong axis, angleshort axis, length
20–40°37-0.16% ± 0.721.06°+3.08% ± 1.09
40–55°37+0.44% ± 0.510.43°+5.62% ± 1.64
55–75°38-1.18% ± 1.180.36°+23.61% ± 20.20

The long axis is measured to well under a percent however side-on the view, and its angle to a fraction of a degree. The short axis is an order of magnitude worse, because that is the direction the protruding parts widen. Distance is read from the long axis and tilt from the ratio of the two — which is exactly why distance stays good in situations that ruin tilt.

Correcting for it

median |tilt error| / bias, degrees, on the 700-pose held-out split. Every model fitted on train only.

model10–20°20–40°40–55°55–71°
none2.36 / -1.762.91 / -2.852.63 / -2.558.52 / -8.52
quadratic1.65 / -0.902.42 / -0.532.65 / +1.813.14 / -2.66
cylinder, fit 5–71° (k=0.0982, floor 11.21°)5.01 / +5.013.42 / +3.423.29 / +3.293.20 / -2.72
cylinder, fit 20–50° (k=0.0433, floor 4.96°)1.82 / +0.982.24 / -0.221.86 / -0.026.00 / -6.00

The one-parameter physical model beats the two-parameter fitted curve — but only when fitted where it applies. Over the full range the mast drags k upward and the result is worse than applying no correction at all.

Re-weighting the outline

Three ways of fitting the ellipse to the same outlines. Each cell is the typical tilt error and the systematic part of it, in degrees.

scheme20–40°40–55°55–75°
A plain3.42 / +2.783.10 / -0.475.79 / -5.79
B symmetric3.54 / +2.593.19 / -0.304.04 / -4.02
C one-sided3.37 / +2.783.08 / -0.073.89 / -3.75

B pays less attention to the parts of the outline nearest the ends of the short axis, which is where the spoiling happens. It loses — because those same points are the only ones that reveal how long the short axis is, so it discards the very measurement it was trying to clean. C instead pays less attention to points that stick outward. That works because the outline can only ever bulge outward, never inward, so “outward” is a reliable sign of trouble while “near the short axis” is not.

A way to get tilt without the short axis at all

The short axis is the unreliable one, so here is a route that never uses it. The <i>angle</i> of the long axis tells each camera which way the robot leans, though not how far; two cameras each supplying that is enough to pin the tilt down completely. Numbers are typical tilt error in degrees. Bands with fewer than five samples in this batch are left blank rather than filled in from an earlier run.

configuration20–40°40–55°55–75°
ratio channel only (shipped)1.34°1.33°--
+ major-axis channel2.21°2.33°--

Off by default, and this table shows why: in the bands the report’s batch actually populates — which are the bands the default rig operates in — the channel makes the normal worse. A dedicated A/B over a wider pose range (90 frames, tilt_max=45°) found it a 2.25× gain at 55–70° and a 1.65× gain overall, so the geometry is sound; what is wrong is the blend weight. Its σ was derived from the precision of ψ in a single view, but the normal comes from a cross product of two and is worse than either, so the channel claims 0.35° against the ratio channel’s 0.45° and outvotes it exactly where the ratio channel is still better. Fitting that σ from measured normal error is the outstanding work. Enable with use_major_channel=True.
